questions.problem:
Given that

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{t}^{n}\} & =\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}, &  & s>0,\end{aligned}
$$

use linearity of Laplace transforms and the first shifting theorem to find the Laplace transform of  $f(t)=5t+3{t}^{2}{e}^{3t}$ for $s>3.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we apply the linearity properties of Laplace transforms:

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{f(t)\} & =L\{5t+3{t}^{2}{e}^{3t}\} \\  & =L\{5t\}+L\{3{t}^{2}{e}^{3t}\} \\  & =5L\{t\}+3L\{{t}^{2}{e}^{3t}\}\end{aligned}
$$

We are given that, for $s>0,$

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{t}^{n}\} & =\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{t\} & =\frac{1}{{s}^{2}} \\ L\{{t}^{2}\} & =\frac{2}{{s}^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

The first shifting theorem states that if $L\{f(t)\}=F(s),$ then $L\{{e}^{at}f(t)\}=F(s-a).$ Therefore,

$$
L\{{t}^{2}{e}^{3t}\}=\frac{2}{(s-3)^{3}}.
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{f(t)\} & =5L\{t\}+3L\{{t}^{2}{e}^{3t}\} \\  & =5\cdot \frac{1}{{s}^{2}}+3\cdot \frac{2}{(s-3)^{3}} \\  & =\frac{5}{{s}^{2}}+\frac{6}{(s-3)^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

This transform is valid for $s>3.$

questions.problem:
Consider a function $y(t)$ such that its Laplace transform is $L\{y(t)\}=Y(s)$ for $s>{s}_{0}.$ Suppose we wish to find $L\{{e}^{4t}y(t)\}.$ Select the correct options in the reasoning below.

By definition of the Laplace transform, we can write 

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{e}^{4t}y(t)\} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-1}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-2}}\,y(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={{field-3}}\,\text{for}\,{{field-4}}.\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Starting from the definition of the Laplace transform, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{e}^{4t}y(t)\} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\cdot {e}^{4t}\,y(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s-4)t}\,y(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall that $Y(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\,y(t)\,\text{d}t,$ where $s>{s}_{0}.$ Therefore, 

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s-4)t}\,y(t)\,\text{d}t=Y(s-4),
$$

where 

$$
s-4>{s}_{0}\,⇒\,s>{s}_{0}+4.
$$

Consider a function $q(t)$ such that its Laplace transform is $L\{q(t)\}=Q(s)$ for $s>{s}_{0}.$ Suppose we wish to find $L\{{e}^{9t}q(t)\}.$ Select the correct options in the reasoning below.

By definition of the Laplace transform, we can write 

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{e}^{9t}q(t)\} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-1}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-2}}\,q(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={{field-3}}\,\text{for}\,{{field-4}}.\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Starting from the definition of the Laplace transform, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{e}^{9t}q(t)\} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\cdot {e}^{9t}\,q(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s-9)t}\,q(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall that $Q(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\,q(t)\,\text{d}t,$ where $s>{s}_{0}.$ Therefore, 

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s-9)t}\,q(t)\,\text{d}t=Q(s-9),
$$

where 

$$
s-9>{s}_{0}\,⇒\,s>{s}_{0}+9.
$$

questions.problem: Consider a function $f(t)$ for which the Laplace transform is $L\{f(t)\}=F(s).$ How can we obtain the graph of $L\{{e}^{-2t}f(t)\}$ from the graph of $F(s)?$
questions.worked_solution:
The first shifting theorem states that if
$L\{f(t)\}=F(s),$
then
$L\{{e}^{at}f(t)\}=F(s-a).$

This implies that multiplying a function $f(t)$ by ${e}^{at}$ shifts the corresponding Laplace transform horizontally along the $s$-axis.

- If $a>0,$ the graph of $F(s)$ shifts to the right.

- If $a<0,$ the graph of $F(s)$ shifts to the left.

In our case, to get the graph of $L\{{e}^{-2t}f(t)\},$ we must shift the graph of $F(s)$ by $2$ units to the left.
